summary: Defines an experimental transport mapping for carrying SNMP over TCP, usable with any SNMP version. It extends the transport mappings in RFC 3417, which centered on UDP, for cases where a reliable connection is wanted.

plainLanguage.summary: Network-management messages usually ride on a fast but unreliable service. This experimental note shows how to send them on a service that makes sure nothing gets lost.

subtitle: Reliable transport for network management messages

tldr.problem: Network management with SNMP typically uses UDP, which does not guarantee delivery. For transferring large amounts of management data, a more reliable approach is needed.
tldr.mechanism: SNMP over TCP uses TCP as the underlying transport protocol instead of UDP. This extends the SNMP transport mappings to support reliable, ordered delivery of management messages.
tldr.outcome: TCP provides reliable delivery and flow control for bulk management data transfer, though SNMP engines must still distinguish between TCP's delivery guarantee and SNMP's application-level confirmation mechanisms.

today: RFC 3430 is an experimental specification. It has not been obsoleted or updated. SNMP over TCP is an optional transport mapping and is less commonly deployed than SNMP over UDP, but is available in many SNMP implementations for bulk transfer scenarios.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3430 defines a transport mapping for the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) over TCP. This extends the transport mappings previously defined in RFC 3417, which centered on UDP, to support sending SNMP messages over TCP when a reliable connection is desired.

SNMP protocol engines that implement this TCP transport mapping MUST also implement the standard SNMP over UDP transport mapping. The TCP mapping is optional and chosen by the application initiating a management transaction based on the requirements of that transaction.
sections.plainLanguage: This document shows how to send network-management messages using reliable mail (TCP) instead of the usual fast but unreliable mail (UDP).

sections.title: SNMP Messages Over TCP
sections.content:
SNMP messages over TCP follow the same structure as UDP-based SNMP. Each message is encoded using BER (Basic Encoding Rules) and sent as a single unit over a TCP connection. An SNMP engine MUST NOT interleave messages within the TCP byte stream; all bytes of one message must be sent before sending bytes of a different message.

Multiple request-response pairs can be exchanged over a single persistent TCP connection. Since TCP is full-duplex, messages can travel in both directions, and responses need not return in the same order as requests were sent. The receiving engine MUST use the length field in the BER-encoded message to separate multiple requests, since TCP may deliver byte sequences that do not align with message boundaries.
sections.plainLanguage: Each management message gets wrapped up and sent whole over the connection. You can send multiple questions and get back multiple answers in any order, as long as you can figure out where each answer ends.

sections.title: Connection Management
sections.content:
TCP connections for SNMP are established on demand by the application that initiates the transaction. Command generator applications open TCP connections to command responder applications; notification originators open connections to notification receiver applications. If the TCP connection cannot be established, the transaction is aborted and reported as a timeout error to the application.

Any SNMP entity can close a TCP connection at any point. This ensures that engines can control resource usage. If a TCP connection closes before a response is received, the sending entity SHOULD signal a timeout error for confirmed operations. The processing of outstanding requests after a TCP connection closes is implementation dependent.

Administrators are recommended to configure SNMP entities to listen on TCP port 161 for command responders and TCP port 162 for notification receivers. An SNMP engine MUST support messages of at least 8192 octets in size.
sections.plainLanguage: The side that wants to talk opens the connection. Either side can hang up. If you hang up before getting an answer, the other side knows you didn't hear back and shouldn't count on you getting the message.

sections.title: Well-Known Ports and Message Size
sections.content:
SNMP over TCP transport addresses use the generic TCP transport domain and address definitions from RFC 3419, which cover both TCP over IPv4 and TCP over IPv6. The recommended well-known port for SNMP command responders is port 161, and port 162 is recommended for notification receivers, matching the ports used for SNMP over UDP.

All SNMP engines using TCP transport MUST be capable of accepting and generating messages that are at least 8192 octets in size. Larger message sizes are encouraged whenever possible to efficiently transfer bulk management data.
sections.plainLanguage: Standardized port numbers help different programs find each other. The minimum message size (8192 bytes) is much bigger than typical UDP messages so you can send large amounts of information efficiently.

sections.title: Reliable Transport Versus Confirmed Operations
sections.content:
While TCP guarantees that delivered data is not damaged, lost, duplicated, or delivered out of order, this is fundamentally different from SNMP's application-level confirmation. A reliable transport like TCP only guarantees that data will reach the remote system; it does not guarantee that the receiving application has processed the data or even received it from the TCP layer.

SNMP protocol operations can be confirmed (like inform-request) or unconfirmed (like snmpV2-trap). With a confirmed operation, the receiving SNMP engine explicitly acknowledges that data was received and may have been processed. Applications requiring confirmation of processing should use SNMP's confirmed operations rather than relying on TCP's transport guarantee alone.

For security, implementors are recommended to use SNMPv3 with the User-based Security Model and View-based Access Control Model to provide proper authentication and access control.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP promises to deliver your message intact, but not that someone read it. If you need to know the manager actually processed your request, ask for a reply in the SNMP protocol itself, not just from TCP.
